title: Near-linear-time exact Euclidean minimum spanning trees
formal: For every fixed integer \(d\ge3\), is there one deterministic algorithm \(A_d\), a constant \(C_d>0\), and an integer \(a_d\ge1\) that compute an exact Euclidean minimum spanning tree of any \(n\ge2\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^d\) in at most \[C_d n\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^{a_d}\] worst-case steps in the real-arithmetic model below? The input is an array of coordinates \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\). The output is a list of \(n-1\) index pairs forming a connected acyclic graph \(T\) minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in T}\|p_i-p_j\|_2\). The program and constants may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates.
why: The problem asks how effectively fixed-dimensional geometry can accelerate one of the most basic graph optimization tasks. Sharp complexity bounds would clarify the algorithmic cost of exact geometric connectivity and its relation to proximity searching.
status_note: The original exact-complexity gap is source-backed. The bounded later-work review through 14 September 2026 did not find matching bounds for the specified deterministic fixed-dimensional family. The 1991 randomized results are dated partial progress, not asserted to be current deterministic records.

sentences: A Euclidean minimum spanning tree connects the input points with minimum total edge length.
The complete graph is implicit in the point coordinates.
The question asks for exact computation in time equal to the number of points times a fixed power of its logarithm.
The guarantee must hold deterministically in every fixed dimension at least three.
Approximate trees and expected-time bounds alone do not meet this target.

definitions: The Euclidean distance is \(\|p-q\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d(p_j-q_j)^2)^{1/2}\). Coordinates are arbitrary exact reals; there is no general-position, bounded-spread or unique-optimum promise. Any minimum tree is a correct output. The complete graph and its edge weights are implicit, so reading every possible edge is not a required part of the input. For each fixed \(d\), the algorithm is one finite deterministic program for all \(n\) and all coordinates, with rational constants, exact real registers and indexed memory. Each operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, nonnegative square root, comparison, copy, indexed read or write costs one step. Addresses and counters are integers of \(O_d(\log(n+t+2))\) bits after \(t\) steps, with ordinary arithmetic and comparisons charged per word operation. There is no floor or bit extraction from real registers, advice depending on the input size, or geometric oracle. All input access and output steps count. Worst-case time is the supremum over all valid size-\(n\) inputs. Constants and programs may depend on fixed \(d\), but not on \(n\) or the coordinates; no simultaneous polynomial dependence on variable dimension is requested.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.

context_blocks.text: The original entry asks whether exact Euclidean MST computation can approach the sorting-scale \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound. At the owner’s request, this card selects an \(n\operatorname{polylog}n\) deterministic worst-case upper bound in each fixed dimension. This is an explicit interpretation of “close,” without requiring the optimal logarithmic exponent.

An MST has only a linear number of edges. Nevertheless, applying a graph algorithm after explicitly creating the complete graph already processes quadratically many candidate edges. The unresolved issue is the cost of identifying the optimum from the much smaller coordinate description.

Agarwal, Edelsbrunner, Schwarzkopf and Welzl relate Euclidean MST computation to bichromatic closest pairs: given red and blue points, find a shortest pair with opposite colors. Their 1991 results include subquadratic expected-time algorithms in fixed dimensions. Those randomized guarantees are not silently assigned to the deterministic model used here.

The plane admits a sorting-scale exact MST algorithm, whereas higher fixed dimensions are the subject of the source question. Large-dimensional distance problems, approximate spanning trees and dynamic maintenance ask for different guarantees.

Cabello, Chan and Giannopoulos study Delaunay triangulations and related MST tasks with predictions in 2026. Their stated setting is planar and includes additional prediction data, so it does not resolve this arbitrary-input higher-dimensional complexity question.

Exactness here refers to the combinatorial tree. In particular, edge ordering can use squared distances because squaring preserves the order of individual nonnegative lengths. This does not require replacing the objective by an approximation or outputting the total length as a decimal number.
